title: Foreground Latency Degradation and Fallback Matrix
author: Maya Patel
summary: Prescriptive strategy and operator runbook for graceful degradation of foreground (latency-sensitive) requests, including a prioritized fallback matrix for model variants, routing policies, dashboard thresholds, and post-incident retro checklist.
body:
Overview

This page documents the operational policy and runbook for handling capacity and performance pressure that threatens foreground latency SLOs (interactive, user-facing requests). It codifies: latency classes, degradation steps and order, a fallback matrix per model family, dashboard/alert thresholds, runbook play-by-play, ownership, and a short retrospective template. The goal is predictable, observable, and auditable degradations that preserve user experience and costs.

Scope

- Applies to: hosted API foreground routes, Redwood Dedicated foreground routes, and Private deployments where Redwood control-plane policies are applied.
- Excludes: background batch jobs, embeddings-only pipelines, async/inference-backfill flows.

Definitions

- Foreground (latency-sensitive): requests where p95 latency impacts UX (chat, single-turn generation API with max_tokens <= 512).
- Latency classes: LOW (p95 <= 200ms), MEDIUM (p95 <= 500ms), HIGH (p95 <= 1500ms).
- Degradation: any automated or manual action that reduces cost, throughput, or fidelity to restore latency SLOs.

SLOs and Alerting Thresholds

- Foreground SLO (global default): p95 latency < 500ms over 5m windows, availability >= 99.9% monthly.
- Per-route overrides should be recorded in the route config catalog.

Alerting (primary):
1) latency-warning: p95 > 500ms for 2 consecutive 60s windows -> Sev4
2) latency-critical: p95 > 1500ms for 1 minute or p99 > 5s -> Sev2
3) capacity-slip: sustained queue length > 2000 requests in router per-region -> Sev2

Diagnostic dashboards (minimum panels)

- p50/p95/p99 by route and model variant (5m, 1h, 24h)
- Request queue length and dequeue rate across routers
- Batch size distribution and batching delay (ms)
- KV cache hit ratio by prefix and tenant
- Model variant CPU/GPU utilization and memory pressure

Fallback Matrix (priority order)

This matrix defines prioritized fallbacks when a route exceeds thresholds. Use automated routing policies first; manual changes are last resort. All model names are logical families; operator must verify compatibility (output shape, tokenization).

| Primary Variant | Fallback A (auto) | Fallback B (auto) | Fallback C (manual) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| rdx-3b-16k-qat | rdx-3b-8k-qat | rdx-3b-8k-int8 | rdx-1.5b-8k-int4 | reduce seq-length, quantize then shrink family |
| rdx-13b-8k | rdx-13b-8k-quant | rdx-7b-8k-quant | rdx-3b-8k-int8 | keep semantic fidelity, stepwise fidelity loss |
| rdx-chat-xl-32k | rdx-chat-xl-16k | rdx-chat-l-16k | rdx-chat-m-8k | preserve chat API schema; prefer sequence length trimming |

Guiding principles:
- Prefer same-architecture fallbacks (quantization, seq-length) before switching family.
- Cache-first: if prefix KV cache has a hit, serve cached response with a header X-Redwood-Degraded: cached-fallback.
- Batching/backoff: for multi-tenant pressure, increase max_batch_ms to trade latency for throughput only if route classified as MEDIUM.

Automated Degradation Policies (Template JSON)

Operators or the autoscaler can apply policies from the policy registry. Example (pseudo-JSON config to apply):

{
  "route_id": "/v1/chat/foreground/standard",
  "triggers": [
    {"metric": "p95_latency_ms", "window": "60s", "threshold": 1500, "action": "step_fallback"},
    {"metric": "router_queue_len", "window": "60s", "threshold": 1000, "action": "throttle_tenant"}
  ],
  "fallback_sequence": ["rdx-13b-8k-quant", "rdx-7b-8k-quant", "rdx-3b-8k-int8"],
  "max_automatic_steps": 2
}

Runbook: operator checklist (ordered)

1) Triage: confirm alert and scope (route(s), region, customers impacted). Check p95/p99 panels and router queue.
2) Short term automated actions (0–2 mins): ensure auto-fallback policy is active; verify policy executed in Routing Audit log.
3) If auto-fallback did not trigger or insufficient (2–10 mins): manually apply preferred fallback via routing console: Route -> Edit -> Fallback Sequence -> Promote next variant.
4) If queues remain > threshold (10–30 mins): apply temporary tenant throttles for noisy tenants as per 'priority-tenant-slicing' policy.
5) If capacity still insufficient (30–90 mins): enable regional burst capacity if available or divert non-critical requests to background queue with async token.
6) Communication: update incident chat channel with: impact summary, routes affected, actions taken. Notify customer-facing teams if SLAs may be affected.
7) Post-stabilization (after p95 returns < SLO for 30m): perform traffic rebalancing, slowly revert fallbacks in reverse order, monitor for regressions.

Manual CLI snippets

- Promote fallback variant (kubectl-like pseudo):
  redwood ctl routing promote --route /v1/chat/foreground/standard --to rdx-13b-8k-quant --reason "latency mitigation"

- Temporarily throttle tenant:
  redwood ctl tenant throttle --tenant-id T-12345 --rate 5r/s --duration 30m --reason "noisy tenant during capacity event"

Ownership and SLAs

- Primary owner: Platform Routing Team (oncall group: platform-routing@redwood).
- Secondary: Serving Runtime (oncall: serving-runtime@redwood).
- Customer communication owner: Customer Success.

Telemetry and Postmortem Data Needs

Capture the following for each incident:
- Timeline of alerts and automated actions (Routing Audit log)
- Per-variant telemetry (latency, utilization, qlen) spanning 1h before -> 2h after
- Snapshot of active autoscaler/cluster state and GPU utilization
- Any manual CLI commands issued and by whom

Acceptance Criteria for Automatic Policies

- Auto-fallback must execute within 90s of trigger and reduce p95 to < SLO within 10 minutes in >= 80% of test-event replays.
- Reversion must be gated by a canary window: 5% traffic for 15 minutes with no p95 regressions.

Runbook: Post-incident retro template

- Summary: one-paragraph incident timeline and impact.
- What went well: automated steps that executed without human intervention.
- What went wrong: missed signals, flaky policies, bad defaults.
- Action items (owner + due date): e.g., add queue-length SLI to route dashboard (Owner: Alice, due: 2026-03-01).
- Verification plan: how we'll validate the fix (load tests, chaos experiments).

Backfill and testing guidance

- Test all fallback sequences in the staging routing cluster during a scheduled chaos run. Use synthetic load that reproduces realistic token/time distributions.
- Add regression tests that verify header X-Redwood-Degraded shows when fallback applied.

Appendix: example incident timeline (abridged)

- 2026-01-22T09:03Z: p95 alert fires for /v1/chat/foreground/standard (p95=2.1s).
- 09:04: auto-fallback policy applied: rdx-13b-8k -> rdx-13b-8k-quant. p95 -> 1.0s.
- 09:10: queue remained high, manual promotion to rdx-7b-8k-quant. p95 -> 480ms.
- 09:45: throttles applied to top 3 noisy tenants.
- 10:30: system stable, reversion plan begun.
